<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README provided, here’s how you can craft a detailed system design diagram that accurately represents Frosty’s architecture:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose  
   • This is a cross-platform mobile and web application built with Flutter. Its purpose is to serve as an alternative Twitch client that supports third-party emotes (7TV, BetterTTV, and FrankerFaceZ) and offers rich, interactive chat features along with live stream browsing.  
   • The README emphasizes its features for enhanced chat readability, state management with MobX, and integration with several external APIs (Twitch, 7TV, BTTV, FFZ).

2. Main Components to Represent  
   • Platforms:  
  – Mobile Platforms: Android and iOS. (Separate directories with native configurations such as Gradle, Xcode projects, and Fastlane for deployments.)  
  – Web Platform: A web version built likely using Next.js (observed in the web folder with components, pages, and assets).  
   • Core Flutter Application: Located in the lib folder, which includes:
  – UI Screens and Widgets: Organized by functional areas (home, channel, chat, video, onboarding, settings, etc.)
  – Business Logic and State Management: MobX stores and corresponding generated files (.g.dart) are used across screens.
  – API Clients: Under lib/apis for interfacing with external services (Twitch, BTTV, 7TV, FFZ).
  – Domain Models: In lib/models, holding key entities like channel, user, stream, badges, etc.
   • External Services and Integrations:  
  – Twitch Developer API (clientId/secret configuration via dart-define)  
  – Third-party emote services (7TV, BTTV, FFZ)  
  – Firebase (firebase_options.dart and firebase_app_id_file.json in iOS)  
   • CI/CD and Deployment Automation:  
  – GitHub workflows (.github/workflows) for CI, pull request checks, release management, etc.
  – Fastlane configurations for both Android and iOS in respective directories.
   • Asset Management:  
  – Assets directory (fonts, icons, images, release notes)  
  – Platform-specific asset management (Android’s res folder, iOS Assets.xcassets)

3. Relationships and Interactions  
   • UI Layer:  
  – Different screens/components (home, channel, chat, video, settings) interact with MobX stores.  
  – Widgets and dialogs receive data from stores, while also triggering actions.
   • Business Logic and State Management:  
  – The MobX stores (in stores directories under each screen set) manage state changes and drive rebuilding of UI components.
   • API Layer and External Communications:  
  – The lib/apis module communicates with Twitch and emote service endpoints.  
  – Data fetched from these APIs is transformed into domain models (from lib/models) and then propagated to the UI via MobX stores.
   • Platform-Specific Integrations:  
  – Android and iOS projects contain native configuration files (e.g., google-services.json, Info.plist) that handle platform-specific services such as Firebase.
   • Continuous Integration/Delivery:  
  – GitHub Actions run tests and builds as configured in .github/workflows.

4. Architectural Patterns and Technologies  
   • Layered/Clean Architecture:  
  – UI components, state management (MobX), and API/data layers are clearly separated.
   • Reactive State Management:  
  – MobX is employed across the application to enable auto-updating of the UI upon state changes.
   • Cross-Platform Best Practices:  
  – Shared business logic across mobile and (potentially) web with Flutter.
   • Development Tooling:  
  – Integration with CI/CD pipelines via GitHub Actions and deployment automation tools (Fastlane).

5. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram  
   • Component Nodes:  
  – Draw nodes for each platform: “Android Client”, “iOS Client”, “Web Client”.  
  – A central “Flutter Core Application” node that includes modules such as “UI Screens & Widgets”, “MobX Stores (State Management)”, “API Clients”, and “Domain Models”.  
  – External Services nodes for “Twitch API”, “7TV / BTTV / FFZ Services”, “Firebase”, etc.
   • Relationships and Interactions:  
  – Use directional arrows to show the flow:
   ○ UI components trigger actions on MobX Stores.
   ○ MobX Stores fetch and update data via the API Clients.
   ○ API Clients interact with External Services.
   ○ Shared assets/configurations (like Firebase and platform-specific resources) supplying services to their respective clients.
   • Visual Aids:  
  – Apply clear labels to each component/subsystem.  
  – Use distinct shapes or color codes to differentiate between mobile, web, and external systems (e.g., rectangles for app modules, cylinders for databases/external services, and clouds for CI/CD pipelines).  
  – Include icons or markers to denote state management (MobX) and API interactions.
   • Detail Level:  
  – Be very detailed in separating components (even if it means creating nodes for each major screen group such as “Chat Module”, “User Authentication”, “Channel / Stream Listing”).  
  – Emphasize the integration flow from user interactions down to API calls and external service responses.
   • Flexibility:  
  – Depending on the audience, you might include optional layers if needed (like data transformation or caching layers), but ensure the core architecture is clearly highlighted.

6. Tailoring the Diagram to Frosty’s Specific Needs  
   • Since Frosty is a de facto full-stack client application (even though the backend services are external), illustrate the separation between the Flutter UI on different platforms and the external APIs it leverages.  
   • Make sure to include annotations on how MobX drives the reactive state management in the application.  
   • Mention the multi-platform nature by showing distinct native configurations (Android, iOS) and the shared Flutter code base.

By following these guidelines, you—as the principal engineer—can create a clear, detailed architecture diagram that encapsulates every essential part of Frosty’s system design, from high-level modules down to the interaction flows between UI, business logic, and external services.
</explanation>
